Inside the Cache: From Silicon to Embedded ML

Anatomy of a Cache Line

A memory address walks into a cache. Here's exactly what happens to it — bit by bit, field by field.

From "fast memory" to actual mechanism

The last post ended on a promise. Caches hold back the memory wall. They do it by guessing that the data you asked for a moment ago, or the data sitting right next to it, is what you'll want next. That's the pitch. It's also the kind of answer that satisfies exactly until someone asks a follow-up: how, mechanically, does the cache know whether it already has what you asked for?

The CPU doesn't walk up to the cache and politely enquire "do you happen to have the value at address 0x7FFC12A4?" There's no conversation. There's a 48-bit (or 64-bit, or 39-bit, depending on the chip) address flying down the bus, and a piece of hardware that has to decide, in a single cycle or two, whether that address lives in the 32 KB of SRAM sitting next to the core. No hash table lookup. No "let me check." A circuit, a couple of comparators, done.

Making that possible is a small feat of engineering, and the whole trick rests on one move: treating an address not as one number, but as three fields stitched together. Once you see the slice, the rest of cache behaviour — associativity, conflict misses, line size tradeoffs — stops feeling mysterious. It starts feeling like arithmetic. That's what this post is about.

A cache lookup isn't a search. It's an arithmetic decomposition of an address into three pieces that each answer a different question.

One example, the whole way through

Rather than wave at "some cache somewhere," we'll pick a single configuration and live with it for the rest of the post. It's the L1 data cache of a typical modern desktop CPU, and the numbers are boring on purpose — they're the ones you'll actually see in datasheets.

  • Cache size: 32 KB (32,768 bytes)
  • Line size: 64 bytes per line
  • Associativity: direct-mapped for now (one line per index)
  • Address width: 32 bits (keeps the arithmetic readable; real x86 uses more)

Divide 32 KB by 64 bytes and you get 512 lines. Each incoming address has to fit itself into one of those 512 slots and prove, once there, that it's actually the right occupant. Those two jobs — figuring out the slot, then checking the occupant — are what the three fields are for.

The offset: which byte inside the line

Start from the bottom of the address. A cache line is 64 bytes. The CPU almost never wants all 64 of them; it wants one specific byte (or word, or cache-line-sized vector — but the pointer it hands you points to a specific byte). Once the line has been located, you still need to know where in the line to look.

To index 64 positions you need log2(64) = 6 bits. So the lowest 6 bits of any address are the offset: which byte within the 64-byte line the CPU actually cares about. This is the easiest field to compute and the easiest to ignore, which is unfortunate, because the offset is the field that turns the line size into a performance parameter. Bigger lines mean more offset bits, more spatial-locality payoff per miss, and more waste if you didn't actually want the neighbours.

Offset bits pick a byte inside a line. They're why spatial locality works at all.

The index: which line slot to look in

Now the harder question. Our cache has 512 lines. When a new address shows up, the hardware needs to instantly pick one of those 512 slots and ask "is the line I want in there?" It can't search all 512. It needs to jump directly to one.

The trick: use some bits of the address as a direct slot number. To pick one of 512 lines you need log2(512) = 9 bits. So the next 9 bits, sitting right above the offset, become the index. Any address whose index bits read as 0b001011010 goes to slot 90. No search, just a wire routing.

This is elegant but has a consequence we'll spend a whole later post on: two completely different memory addresses can share the same index. They'll both want the same slot. The cache can only hold one at a time, and they'll fight — that's a conflict, and it's why associativity was invented. For now, though, we just note that index selects the slot.

The tag: proving you're the right occupant

Once you've gone to slot 90, you still don't know whether the line sitting there is your line. Many addresses map to slot 90 — specifically, every address whose middle bits are 0b001011010, regardless of the upper bits. One of them currently lives there. You need to check which.

The remaining high bits of the address — the ones that weren't used for index or offset — are the tag. The cache line stores, alongside the actual data, a copy of the tag that was there when the line was loaded. To verify a match, the hardware compares your address's tag bits against the stored tag. Equal? Cache hit, serve the byte. Not equal? Cache miss, go ask the next level down.

With 32-bit addresses, 6 offset bits and 9 index bits, that leaves 32 − 9 − 6 = 17 bits of tag. Every line in the cache carries a 17-bit tag in addition to its 64 bytes of data. That storage overhead is real. We'll count it properly in a moment.

Tag says "who I am." Index says "where I live." Offset says "which byte to hand over."

Putting it together

A 32-bit address in our cache reads, from high bit to low bit, as:

The split, for 32 KB cache · 64 B line · direct-mapped
[ TAG : 17 bits ][ INDEX : 9 bits ][ OFFSET : 6 bits ]
bits 31 down to 15 · bits 14 down to 6 · bits 5 down to 0

Try it with a real address. Take 0x000ABCDE. That's 0000 0000 0000 1010 1011 1100 1101 1110 in binary. Slice off the bottom 6 bits (011110) and you get offset 30. The next 9 bits (011110011) give index 243. Everything above that (00000000000010101) is tag 21. The interactive below will do this for you, but I'd encourage you to do one by hand first. It's the kind of thing you only need to do once before it clicks.

Notice what happens with 0x00001040 and 0x00009040. Different addresses, different tags. But look at their index bits — identical. They fight for slot 65. Back-to-back access to both, and every access misses, because each one kicks the other out. A whole class of slowdowns lives in that collision, and we'll spend Post 3 on it.

What a line actually stores

So far we've talked about the address. Let's look at what's sitting in the slot.

A cache line is more than its 64 bytes of data. Alongside those bytes, the cache hardware keeps a small bundle of metadata: the tag (17 bits, in our case), a valid bit saying whether this slot currently holds real data or just garbage left over from reset, and a dirty bit saying whether the line has been written to since being loaded (which matters when it eventually gets evicted — an untouched line can just be dropped, a dirty one has to be written back). There may also be coherence-state bits for multicore systems, but those belong to Post 6.

Do the arithmetic. 64 bytes of data is 512 bits. Add 17 for the tag, 1 for valid, 1 for dirty. 531 bits per line, of which 512 are data and 19 are overhead. Multiply by 512 lines and the cache holds 512 × 531 = 271,872 bits of SRAM, of which 262,144 bits (32 KB) are advertised as the cache size. The rest is the price of the lookup machinery. About 3.6% overhead. Reasonable.

The "32 KB" on the datasheet is just the payload. The tag array, the valid bits, the comparators — those are all real silicon too.

Watching a miss pull in its neighbours

Now the part that was promised in Post 1 and never quite shown. When the CPU asks for one byte and it's not in the cache, the cache doesn't just fetch that one byte. It fetches the entire 64-byte line the byte belongs to. One miss, one trip to DRAM, sixty-four bytes delivered. The byte you wanted gets handed to the CPU. The other sixty-three sit in the line, waiting, in case you want them next.

That "in case you want them" is spatial locality collecting its interest. A sequential array walk asks for byte 0, pays the full miss cost, and the hardware helpfully brings back bytes 1 through 63 as a bonus. The next sixty-three reads are hits. The program feels fast, and it's fast because the hardware bet correctly that a loop was going to keep walking forward. Flip to a random-access pattern and the sixty-three bonus bytes almost never get used — you pay a full miss for every single access. Same code, same arithmetic, wildly different outcome. That was the lesson of Post 1. This is the mechanism behind it.

Click Request a byte to pull in a line. Then click Next byte a few times and watch every request hit without a new fetch — that's spatial locality paying out.

The line slot holds 64 bytes: the one you asked for (gold), plus its 63 neighbours (green). Sequential follow-up reads land on green bytes and never touch DRAM. Jump to a far address and you invalidate the tag, kick the whole line out, and pay the miss cost again. A miss isn't 64 individual misses, and it isn't one byte — it's one trip that brings back a chunk. How much of that chunk you actually use is what separates fast code from slow code.

Line size is a tradeoff, not a constant

We've been saying "64 bytes" as if it were a law of physics. It isn't. Line size is a design choice, and it's a tradeoff, which means you can get it wrong in either direction.

Larger lines (say, 128 bytes) amortise the miss cost across more neighbours. If your workload is streaming through an array, every miss buys you twice as many free hits, and throughput climbs. On the other hand, larger lines bring back more data you might not actually use, which wastes memory bandwidth and pollutes the cache with bytes that end up evicted without ever being read. On embedded targets with tight memory buses, this is a real penalty — you're spending bandwidth you don't have on data you don't want.

Smaller lines (say, 32 bytes) are the opposite. Each miss is cheaper, less bandwidth gets wasted on unused bytes, and the cache holds more distinct lines for the same total size. But you lose the spatial-locality bonus; a sequential walk pays twice as many misses, and miss-handling overhead starts to dominate.

64 bytes emerged as the industry consensus because it lines up with a typical DRAM burst transfer, works well for the access patterns of most real programs, and balances the two extremes. It's not sacred. ARM cores often use 32- or 64-byte lines depending on the generation. GPU caches can go up to 128 bytes. DSPs sometimes use 16. The right answer is workload-dependent, which is exactly why cache design is a specialty and not a solved problem.

Every cache parameter is a bet about what your programs are going to do. Line size is the bet about how far "next" usually is.

Why the bit split has to be in that order

A small thing worth pointing out before we close. The fields have to be arranged as [ TAG | INDEX | OFFSET ], in that order, from high bits to low. It's not arbitrary. It's a direct consequence of what each field does.

Offset has to be in the low bits because consecutive bytes in memory differ only in their low bits. Two addresses one byte apart must land in the same cache line with different offsets — otherwise spatial locality would break. Index has to sit right above offset because adjacent lines should land in adjacent slots, which keeps the index from being trivially aliased by small strides. And tag takes the leftover high bits because that's what's left over, and because the high bits vary slowly, which gives the comparator something consistent to check.

Flip the order — put the tag in the low bits, say — and a stride-1 array walk suddenly spreads across different tags inside a single line, which is nonsense. The layout isn't a preference, it's a constraint.

Where this is going

You now know what the hardware is actually doing when your code accesses memory. An address arrives. Bottom 6 bits say "which byte." Next 9 bits say "which slot." Top 17 bits get compared to whatever's sitting in that slot. If the tags match and the valid bit is set, the right byte gets pulled out of the 64-byte line and handed back in roughly a single cycle. If not, the whole line gets refilled from the next level, and the CPU waits.

We did all of this with one simplifying assumption: one line per index. That's called direct-mapped, and it has a well-known pathology. Two addresses with the same index bits can't both live in the cache, even if there's plenty of unused space in other slots. That's an expensive problem, and the next post is the solution. Associativity is what happens when you let a slot hold more than one line, and it's how every real cache in your laptop actually works.

A direct-mapped cache is the clean version of the idea. The real versions are messier, and the mess is what makes them fast.
